summary: A fifty-one minute peer role-play, roughly a third of it small talk about Michael's living situation in Florianopolis, meal prep, and languages. The drill proper runs twice. First Michael closes and Richard plays a prospect with a spouse objection that converts into fear: Michael runs the responsibility frame, the bridge, the plane and the boiling-frog analogies, twice loses his place in the script, and never asks for the sale — Richard's debrief note is that he should have gone for the close far earlier. They then swap, and Richard closes Michael on a pure money objection, running isolation, the should-versus-how reframe, monthly surplus, savings and available credit, and landing on a split payment. The call ends with the two of them discovering they disagree about the company's own interest terms and having to work it out between themselves.
notable: THE PAYMENT PLAN TERMS ARE NOT KNOWN BY THE PEOPLE SELLING THEM — after Richard closes on a split, Michael tells him to disclose interest and gives a figure he is guessing at: 'you're gonna have to find a way to bring up the interest, because it is an extra like 300 bucks or something for payment, I think, if I remember correct.' Richard gives a different one: 'through a financer, it's a little less, I mean, but through ourselves, it's like 200 a month extra.' Richard then states 'Two and three payments doesn't have interest, by the way', Michael contradicts him — 'I'm pretty sure three does, dude' — Richard checks and Michael concedes 'Three payments of 2,000. Just kidding and take it back.' Michael closes with 'Yeah, okay, cool. didn't know that.' He took live sales calls the same day.

THE STRUCTURE, ONCE ESTABLISHED, IS EXPLICIT AND STANDARD — 'ideally you go for two, if really needed, then you can push them to Free, but after that, it's interest.' Two payments of $3,000 or three of $2,000 carry no interest; anything longer does. This directly contradicts the line the sales manager scripted three days earlier — 'we don't have any sort of set payment plans at all. It just really depends on what we can make work with the person.' Standard tiers with a defined interest threshold plainly exist.

A REP DESCRIBED RUNNING NINETY MINUTES OF OBJECTION HANDLING AND SEVEN WORD TRACKS ON A FRIGHTENED PROSPECT — Richard, arguing that going for the close early is better: 'I have been on MooseMath and I've done like a one and a half hour objection handling. I've done like seven of those stupid word tracks or however you call it. Every single time I was like, yeah, I know I need to do it, but man, it's, it's, just scared.' The prospect had a hospital history, no progress in ten years, and, in Richard's words, 'you don't really have the money. It's even worse.'

THE FEAR TRACK AS REHEARSED USES SHAME AND TAKE-AWAY — 'Or we crumble and we retreat and we go right back to where we're at today and settle for mediocrity with all due respect'; 'Are you sure? Because it kind of doesn't seem like it, dude, even just with how you're saying it... and it's okay if you don't want to do it. Like, it really is. Like, that's what most people do. Most people don't'; 'do you want to be the version of Richard that crumbles every time there's a challenge?' The rehearsed uncertainty reframe also uses the prospect's marriage proposal as the analogy for a $6,000 purchase.

THE SPOUSE-EXCLUSION PLAY RUN AGAIN, THIS TIME LEVERAGING THE WIFE'S PROFESSION — the role-play wife is a nurse, and the move is 'if something happens in hospital, like a patient shows up in the ER... I'm assuming she doesn't call you and ask you, you know, run to you to ask how to do her job', landing on 'why do you feel like it's fair for you to run to her and ask her to make a decision on something that ultimately she doesn't fully know about'. Same structure as the 07/06 rehearsal, now with the spouse's competence as the lever.

MICHAEL LOST THE SCRIPT TWICE MID-DRILL — 'I'm blanking now. . Give me a second. What's the next thing? Let me just look real quick' and 'No, I'm forgetting again. Sakes.' He also never asked for the sale; Richard's whole debrief was 'you just need to go for the close.' He had a live prospect call booked an hour later.

BOTH CLOSERS WERE UNDER ACUTE PERSONAL REVENUE PRESSURE THE SAME WEEK AS THE CALLS IN THIS BATCH — Michael: 'dude, I need to close a couple deals like ASAP, bro', 'I just need to get my money stacked up again', 'I just want to get to a point where I'm making at least 12K on this offer.' Richard: 'I need another four to hit my projections.'

MANAGER 1-1s CONTINUE TO GO INTO PERSONAL PSYCHOLOGICAL TERRITORY, AND THE REP EXPERIENCES IT AS THERAPY — Richard on his session with Chris Klevan minutes earlier: 'bro, you should become, like, a coach or something... it was quite deep very quickly, but now I just have to let it go' and 'Within like a few minutes, he just got to the core. I can't find the core myself where I really have to question, but I try to steer away from it always. But he got to the core of why I have all of this in like five minutes.' Michael: 'Yeah, Chris is good at that, dude.'

Richard's stated close philosophy is to ask early and often — 'sometimes going for a close, what's the worst thing? Maybe they say, ah, but I don't know. They can just go in again.' Michael disagrees on evidence he does not produce: 'I think you underestimate that when you put responses, because I've done these types of clothes a lot.'

Working conditions: Michael is in Florianopolis, Brazil in an unheated short-let with no reliable power point, a bright kitchen table, and internet that froze the call for over a minute and dropped it entirely for two minutes. He is considering taking prospect calls outdoors on Wi-Fi. Richard is in Bulgaria.
Michael attributes 'We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence then is not an act, but a habit' to Socrates, and reads it off screen mid-drill.
